stem: A 63-year-old woman develops fever, flank pain and hypotension 10 minutes into a red cell transfusion. Her urine turns wine-colored and her plasma is pink after centrifugation. The transfusion is stopped.
oneliner: 63F + fever, flank pain, hypotension minutes into transfusion + wine-colored urine + pink plasma → which lab falls?
ask: Which laboratory value is expected to be decreased?

whyNot.A: **Rises** as red cells lyse and release the enzyme
whyNot.B: **Rises** from heme breakdown, though more slowly
whyNot.D: Responds days later; it is not expected to fall, and a **pink plasma** points to free hemoglobin
whyNot.E: **Rises**: it is what turns the plasma pink

answer: Serum haptoglobin (it binds free hemoglobin and is cleared)
why: **Fever, flank pain and hypotension during a transfusion** with **dark urine** is an acute hemolytic reaction (ABO mismatch), an **intravascular** hemolysis. Lysed cells release **free hemoglobin** and **LDH**, and **unconjugated bilirubin** follows; **haptoglobin** binds the free hemoglobin and is **used up**, so it falls.

idea.rule: Intravascular hemolysis: haptoglobin falls; LDH, free hemoglobin and unconjugated bilirubin rise, with hemoglobinuria.
also: Hemoglobinuria and hemosiderinuria appear in intravascular hemolysis
Spherocytes and a positive Coombs test point to extravascular, antibody-mediated hemolysis
Other intravascular causes: G6PD crisis, PNH, mechanical valve, DIC
Delayed hemolytic reaction (week later) is mostly extravascular

stem: A 58-year-old man has had painless cervical lymphadenopathy for 4 months. DNA from the node and from his buccal epithelium is digested and run on a Southern blot with an immunoglobulin heavy-chain J-region probe. The epithelial lane shows one band, while the node lane shows that band plus a single additional band of a different size.
oneliner: 58M + painless cervical nodes + IgH J-region Southern blot: epithelium 1 band, node same band plus one extra band → interpretation?
ask: Which interpretation of the node result is correct?

options.B: No Ig gene rearrangement in the node
options.D: Normal class switching in germinal-center B cells

whyNot.A: Each of many small clones is too rare to make its own band, so a reactive node shows **no distinct extra band**
whyNot.B: The **extra band** in the node lane means rearranged Ig DNA is present
whyNot.C: The probe detects the **immunoglobulin heavy-chain** locus, so it reports B-cell, not T-cell, rearrangement
whyNot.D: Switching happens independently in many B cells and alters constant-region genes; it would not give **one dominant J-region band**

answer: A clonal (monoclonal) B-cell population: one dominant rearranged IgH band
why: Every B cell rearranges its Ig genes in its own way, so **non-B cells keep only the germline band**. A **single extra band** means a large share of the cells carry the **same rearrangement**: a **clonal B-cell** expansion such as follicular lymphoma. In a reactive node each clone is too small to detect, so only the **germline band** (at most a faint smear) is seen.

idea.rule: A distinct rearranged Ig band = one B-cell clone; germline band alone or a smear = polyclonal.
also: The same logic with TCR probes tests T-cell clonality
PCR for IgH rearrangement gives one dominant peak in a clone
Flow cytometry showing a single light chain (κ or λ) also marks a B-cell clone
Light-chain restriction in plasma cells marks myeloma or MGUS

stem: A 79-year-old woman is asymptomatic. Routine serum protein electrophoresis shows a narrow-based spike in the gamma region. The M protein is IgG at 1.8 g/dL, with normal IgA and IgM, and her urine has no light chains. Hemoglobin, calcium and creatinine are normal, and a bone marrow biopsy shows 6% plasma cells.
oneliner: 79F + asymptomatic + narrow gamma spike, IgG M protein 1.8 g/dL + normal IgA, IgM + no urine light chains + normal Hb, Ca, Cr + marrow 6% plasma cells → interpretation?
ask: Which interpretation of the electrophoresis finding is correct?

whyNot.A: Inflammation gives a **broad-based polyclonal** rise, not a narrow spike
whyNot.B: Also produces a **broad polyclonal** gammopathy, not a single narrow band
whyNot.D: Needs **≥10% marrow plasma cells** or end-organ damage; she has **6%** and normal Hb, Ca and Cr
whyNot.E: Produces an **IgM** spike; hers is IgG

answer: MGUS (a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance)
why: A **narrow spike** means **one plasma-cell clone** making a single immunoglobulin, whereas chronic inflammation or liver disease gives a **broad polyclonal** band. With M protein **under 3 g/dL**, **under 10% marrow plasma cells** and **no CRAB features**, this is **MGUS**. About 1% per year progress to myeloma.

idea.rule: Narrow M spike = one clone; broad gamma band = polyclonal reaction. Then count plasma cells and organ damage.
also: Myeloma: ≥10% plasma cells or CRAB features (hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia, bone lesions)
Smoldering myeloma: M protein ≥3 g/dL or 10-60% plasma cells without CRAB
Polyclonal gammopathy: chronic infection, autoimmune disease, cirrhosis

stem: A 32-year-old woman has felt tired for four months and looks pale. She has soaked through a pad every two hours during her periods since last year. Hemoglobin is 10 g/dL, MCV is 73 fL and the red cell distribution width is raised; the smear shows hypochromic cells with enlarged central pallor.
oneliner: 32F + fatigue, pallor + heavy menses + Hb 10, MCV 73, high RDW, hypochromic cells → which iron studies?
ask: Which set of iron studies is most likely?

options.A: Low ferritin, low serum iron, low TIBC
options.B: High ferritin, low serum iron, low TIBC
options.C: Low ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC
options.D: High ferritin, high serum iron, high transferrin saturation
options.E: Normal ferritin, normal serum iron, high HbA2

whyNot.A: **Low TIBC** is wrong: with empty stores the liver makes more transferrin, so TIBC rises
whyNot.B: **Chronic disease** pattern (high ferritin, low TIBC); her ongoing blood loss depletes stores instead
whyNot.D: **Iron overload** pattern (hemochromatosis); she is losing iron every month, not accumulating it
whyNot.E: **Beta-thalassemia trait**: normal iron studies with raised HbA2; her menstrual losses point to a true deficit

answer: Low ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC and low transferrin saturation (iron deficiency anemia)
why: Chronic blood loss empties iron stores, so **ferritin falls first** and serum iron follows. The liver raises transferrin, which gives a **high TIBC** and a **low saturation**; the marrow makes small, pale cells with a **high RDW**.

idea.rule: Iron deficiency = low ferritin, low iron, high TIBC, low saturation.
also: Chronic disease: ferritin high, iron low, TIBC low
Iron overload: ferritin high, saturation high
Marrow iron stain absent in deficiency
Plummer-Vinson: dysphagia and esophageal web with iron deficiency

stem: A 46-year-old woman has felt tired for two months and bruises easily. She has a fullness under the left ribs, and the spleen tip reaches the pelvic brim. White cell count is 120,000/mm3 with neutrophils, myelocytes and metamyelocytes, and she has had no fever or recent infection. Smear shows no toxic granulation.
oneliner: 46F + fatigue, bruising + massive splenomegaly + WBC 120,000 with myelocytes, no infection → which lab finding?
ask: Which laboratory finding best separates her condition from a leukemoid reaction?

options.E: 20% or more myeloblasts with Auer rods

whyNot.B: **High LAP** is the leukemoid reaction; with no infection and a huge spleen she has a clonal disorder
whyNot.C: **Toxic granulation and Dohle bodies** accompany infection; the smear here shows none
whyNot.D: **Atypical lymphocytes** suggest mononucleosis; her excess cells are myeloid
whyNot.E: **Blast crisis or AML** needs 20% or more blasts; hers are mature and maturing forms

answer: Low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score (chronic myeloid leukemia)
why: Neutrophilia with **immature forms and a huge spleen** without infection suggests **CML**. The malignant neutrophils lack the enzyme, so the **LAP score is low**, whereas reactive neutrophils in a leukemoid reaction have a **high LAP score**.

idea.rule: CML = low LAP; leukemoid reaction = high LAP.

stem: A 19-year-old man with sickle cell disease has had two days of yellow eyes and dark urine after a painful crisis. Hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL and the reticulocyte count is elevated. A dipstick of the urine is negative for bilirubin, and ultrasound previously showed gallstones that are pigmented and black.
oneliner: 19M + sickle cell disease + jaundice + dark urine without urinary bilirubin + reticulocytosis → which serum panel?
ask: Which set of serum findings reflects his ongoing process?

options.A: High haptoglobin, high LDH, high conjugated bilirubin
options.B: Low haptoglobin, normal LDH, high conjugated bilirubin
options.C: High haptoglobin, low LDH, normal bilirubin
options.D: Normal haptoglobin, high alkaline phosphatase, high conjugated bilirubin
options.E: Low haptoglobin, high LDH, high unconjugated bilirubin

whyNot.A: **High haptoglobin** is wrong: free hemoglobin binds and consumes it; **conjugated** bilirubin would appear in urine, and his urine has none
whyNot.B: **Normal LDH** is wrong: red cells rich in LDH are bursting; conjugated bilirubin would also colour the urine
whyNot.C: **Normal bilirubin** cannot give jaundice; haptoglobin is **consumed**, not raised, in hemolysis
whyNot.D: **Cholestatic** pattern (raised alkaline phosphatase, conjugated bilirubin) causes bilirubinuria, which he lacks

answer: Low haptoglobin, high LDH and high unconjugated bilirubin (hemolysis)
why: Breaking red cells release hemoglobin that **consumes haptoglobin** and floods the blood with **LDH**. Heme is converted to **unconjugated bilirubin**, which is albumin-bound and not filtered, so the urine has none, and the marrow answers with **reticulocytosis**.

idea.rule: Hemolysis = haptoglobin down, LDH up, unconjugated bilirubin up.
also: Acholuric jaundice: no bilirubin in urine
Pigment gallstones form from chronic hemolysis
Intravascular hemolysis also gives hemoglobinuria and hemosiderinuria

stem: A 15-year-old girl has monthly periods that last 10 days and need a change of pad every hour. She has frequent nosebleeds, and her gums bleed after brushing. Her mother needed packing after a dental extraction, and her maternal grandfather bled for days after a minor surgery. Her joints are normal and she has no bruising of deep muscles.
oneliner: 15F + menorrhagia, epistaxis, gum bleeding + mother bled after dental extraction → which coagulation profile?
ask: Which set of screening results is most likely?

options.A: Normal bleeding time, normal PT, prolonged PTT
options.B: Prolonged bleeding time, normal platelets, normal PT, borderline PTT
options.C: Prolonged bleeding time, low platelet count, normal PTT
options.D: Normal bleeding time, prolonged PT, normal PTT
options.E: Prolonged bleeding time, prolonged PT, prolonged PTT, low fibrinogen

whyNot.A: **Hemophilia** pattern; it affects males, gives joint and muscle bleeds, and spares the bleeding time
whyNot.C: **ITP** pattern: mucosal bleeding, but a low platelet count and no dominant family history
whyNot.D: **Isolated PT prolongation** (factor VII or vitamin K lack) leaves the bleeding time normal; her mucosal bleeding with a dominant family pattern points to a platelet adhesion defect
whyNot.E: **DIC**: all screens abnormal with low fibrinogen, in a very ill patient; she is well

answer: Prolonged bleeding time with normal platelet count and PT, and a normal or mildly prolonged PTT (von Willebrand disease)
why: Mucosal bleeding in a family with **dominant inheritance** points to **von Willebrand disease**. Missing vWF impairs **platelet adhesion**, so the bleeding time is long; vWF also carries factor VIII, so the **PTT may be mildly prolonged**, and PT and platelet count are normal.

idea.rule: vWD = long bleeding time, normal platelets and PT, PTT normal or borderline.
also: vWF carries and protects factor VIII

stem: A 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis for twenty years has felt tired for several months. Hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL, MCV is 84 fL and the reticulocyte count is low. She has no bleeding, takes no iron and eats a normal diet. Her joints are warm and swollen, and ESR is raised.
oneliner: 60F + long-standing rheumatoid arthritis + fatigue + Hb 10.4, MCV 84, low reticulocytes → which iron studies and marrow stain?
ask: Which set of iron studies and marrow iron findings is most likely?

options.A: Low iron, high TIBC, low ferritin, absent marrow iron
options.B: Low iron, low TIBC, low ferritin, absent marrow iron
options.C: High iron, high saturation, high ferritin, ring sideroblasts
options.D: Low iron, low TIBC, high ferritin, iron in marrow macrophages
options.E: Normal iron, normal ferritin, normal marrow iron, raised HbA2

whyNot.A: **Iron deficiency** pattern (high TIBC, absent stores); she has no blood loss or poor intake
whyNot.B: **Low ferritin** with absent marrow iron means true deficiency; inflammation instead keeps ferritin up
whyNot.C: **Ring sideroblasts** with high serum iron come from blocked heme synthesis; her only illness is active rheumatoid arthritis, which lowers serum iron
whyNot.E: **Thalassemia trait**: microcytic with high HbA2; her MCV is normal

answer: Low serum iron and TIBC with normal or high ferritin, and marrow iron trapped in macrophages (anemia of chronic disease)
why: Chronic inflammation raises **hepcidin**, which blocks ferroportin and **traps iron in macrophages**. Serum iron and **TIBC fall**, ferritin (an acute phase protein) stays **normal or high**, and the marrow stain shows iron in macrophages but little reaching red cell precursors.

idea.rule: Anemia of chronic disease = hepcidin up, iron trapped, ferritin high, TIBC low.
also: Treat the underlying disease; erythropoietin may help
Ferritin is an acute phase reactant

stem: A 35-year-old woman is started on an unfractionated heparin infusion for a deep vein thrombosis of the left leg. Her platelet count is 200,000/mm3 at the start. On day 7 the count is 90,000/mm3, the calf is more swollen and a new area of pain appears in the other leg. She has no bleeding, and her PT is normal.
oneliner: 35F + DVT on unfractionated heparin + platelets 200,000 to 90,000 on day 7 + new thrombosis, no bleeding → which test confirms the cause?
ask: Which test is most likely to confirm the cause of the platelet fall?

whyNot.A: **Anti-GPIIb/IIIa** antibodies confirm ITP, which does not cause thrombosis and has no heparin link
whyNot.C: **ADAMTS13** is low in TTP, with schistocytes, fever and neurologic or renal signs; none are described
whyNot.D: **Coombs test** detects antibodies on red cells, not platelets
whyNot.E: **Fibrinogen and D-dimer** assess DIC; a normal PT and no bleeding argue against it

answer: Antibody assay for heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia)
why: A platelet fall of **more than 50% at 5 to 10 days** after heparin, with **new thrombosis** and no bleeding, indicates **HIT**. Heparin binds platelet factor 4 and forms **IgG-bound complexes** that activate platelets; the **anti-PF4/heparin antibody** assay confirms it.

idea.rule: HIT = platelets down more than 50% at days 5 to 10, thrombosis, anti-PF4/heparin IgG.
also: Stop heparin and give a direct thrombin inhibitor such as argatroban
Platelet activation causes thrombosis, not bleeding
Warfarin alone can worsen it by lowering protein C

stem: A 3-month-old boy is fed formula mixed with water from a private well. Today his lips and fingertips look blue-gray. He is lethargic but has no cough or increased work of breathing. Chest x-ray and echocardiogram are normal. Blood drawn for testing looks dark brown and does not redden when shaken in air.
oneliner: 3-mo M + formula made with well water + cyanosis + normal chest x-ray and echo + chocolate-brown blood → which blood gas and oximetry pattern?
ask: Which arterial blood gas and oximetry pattern is most likely?

options.A: Normal PaO2, oximetry near 85% unchanged by oxygen
options.B: Low PaO2 and low saturation that rise with oxygen
options.C: Normal PaO2 and normal saturation with low hemoglobin
options.D: Low PaO2 with oximetry reading near 100%
options.E: Normal PaO2 and normal oximetry with raised carboxyhemoglobin

whyNot.B: **Lung disease or shunt** pattern; his chest x-ray and echo are normal, and the colour does not change with oxygen
whyNot.C: **Anemia** has a normal saturation and pallor, not cyanosis
whyNot.D: **Low PaO2 with near-100% oximetry** is not physiologic; without an abnormal hemoglobin, saturation follows PaO2
whyNot.E: **Carbon monoxide** gives a cherry-red colour and bright red blood; his skin is blue-gray and his blood dark brown

answer: Normal PaO2 with oximetry saturation near 85% that does not improve with oxygen (methemoglobinemia)
why: Nitrates in well water, a risk in young infants, oxidize iron to the **ferric state**, forming **methemoglobin**, which cannot carry oxygen and gives **chocolate-brown blood**. Dissolved oxygen is unchanged so **PaO2 is normal**, but oximetry is pulled toward about **85%** and does not respond to oxygen.

idea.rule: Methemoglobinemia = normal PaO2, saturation gap near 85%, no response to oxygen.
also: Fe3+ shifts the oxygen curve to the left
Carbon monoxide: cherry-red skin and falsely high oximetry

stem: A 49-year-old man has a painful blue-tinged index finger with intact radial and ulnar pulses. He also has had nosebleeds recently. Platelet count is 1,530,000/mm3 with normal hemoglobin, MCV and white cell count. He has no fever, weight loss, inflammation or known cancer, and has never had surgery.
oneliner: 49M + painful blue finger with full pulses + nosebleeds + platelets 1.53 million, normal Hb, MCV and WBC + no inflammation → which finding supports a primary cause?
ask: Which finding best supports a primary over a reactive thrombocytosis?

options.C: Raised red cell mass, low erythropoietin
options.E: Teardrop cells with a dry tap

whyNot.A: **Absent iron** gives a reactive thrombocytosis from iron deficiency; his hemoglobin and MCV are normal
whyNot.B: **BCR-ABL1** defines CML, which brings a high white cell count; his is normal
whyNot.C: **Raised red cell mass** is polycythemia vera; his hemoglobin is normal
whyNot.E: **Teardrop cells with a dry tap** are myelofibrosis, with anemia and a big spleen; not described

answer: Clusters of large, hyperlobulated megakaryocytes with normal iron stores (essential thrombocythemia)
why: Platelets above a million with **both thrombosis and bleeding** and no secondary cause point to **essential thrombocythemia**. The marrow shows **megakaryocytic hyperplasia**, often with **JAK2**, CALR or MPL mutations, and **normal iron stores**; reactive causes include iron deficiency and inflammation.

idea.rule: Essential thrombocythemia = platelets over 1 million, megakaryocytes, normal Hb and WBC, no BCR-ABL1.

stem: A 45-year-old man who is homeless and drinks heavily has felt weak for three months. Hemoglobin is 8.5 g/dL with an MCV of 110 fL, and neutrophils on the smear have six or more lobes. Red cell folate is low and serum vitamin B12 is normal. He has normal vibration sense and gait.
oneliner: 45M + homeless, alcohol use + macrocytic anemia + hypersegmented neutrophils + low red cell folate, normal B12, no neurologic signs → which MMA and homocysteine?
ask: Which pair of methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels is most likely?

whyNot.A: **Both raised** is the B12 pattern; his B12 is normal and he has no neurologic signs
whyNot.B: **Raised MMA** needs B12 deficiency, and his B12 is normal
whyNot.D: **Both normal** would not explain macrocytosis; folate lack stalls remethylation of homocysteine
whyNot.E: **Low homocysteine** is the opposite; failed conversion to methionine causes homocysteine to accumulate

answer: Normal methylmalonic acid with increased homocysteine (folate deficiency)
why: Folate supplies the methyl group that **converts homocysteine to methionine**, so deficiency causes **high homocysteine**. **Methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA** needs only B12, so MMA stays **normal**; with B12 deficiency both rise and neurologic signs appear.

idea.rule: Folate deficiency = homocysteine up, MMA normal; B12 deficiency = both up.
also: B12 deficiency adds subacute combined degeneration
Folate stores last months; B12 stores last years
Folic acid alone can mask B12 deficiency

stem: A 6-year-old boy has had repeated nosebleeds and bleeding gums since infancy. He bled for a long time after losing a tooth. His parents are first cousins, and a brother has similar symptoms. He takes no medicines. Platelet count, platelet size, PT and PTT are all normal.
oneliner: 6M + lifelong nosebleeds and gum bleeding + prolonged bleeding after tooth loss + consanguinity + normal platelets, PT, PTT → which platelet aggregation pattern?
ask: Which platelet aggregation study pattern is most likely?

options.A: Absent ristocetin agglutination with normal ADP aggregation
options.B: Absent ristocetin agglutination corrected by normal plasma
options.C: No aggregation to ADP, collagen or thrombin; ristocetin normal
options.D: Normal aggregation to all agonists with low platelet count
options.E: Absent aggregation to arachidonic acid only

whyNot.A: **Absent ristocetin response** with normal ADP fits Bernard-Soulier, which has giant platelets and a low count; his count and size are normal
whyNot.B: **Correction by normal plasma** is von Willebrand disease, usually dominant with an affected parent; his parents are well and related, pointing to recessive inheritance
whyNot.D: **Normal aggregation** with low count is ITP; his count is normal
whyNot.E: **Arachidonic acid only** fits aspirin or a cyclooxygenase defect; he takes no medicines and his disease is lifelong and recessive

answer: No aggregation to ADP, collagen or thrombin with normal ristocetin agglutination (Glanzmann thrombasthenia)
why: Mucosal bleeding with a **normal platelet count** and **autosomal recessive** inheritance suggests **Glanzmann thrombasthenia**. The **GpIIb/IIIa** receptor is absent, so platelets cannot bridge via fibrinogen and fail to aggregate with ADP, collagen or thrombin; **ristocetin agglutination**, which depends on GpIb, is normal.

idea.rule: Glanzmann = GpIIb/IIIa defect: no aggregation to agonists, ristocetin normal.
also: Bernard-Soulier: GpIb defect, giant platelets, low count, no ristocetin response

stem: A 7-month-old boy of Italian descent was well at birth but has become pale and irritable over the past two months. He has frontal bossing, and the liver and spleen are enlarged. Hemoglobin is 5.8 g/dL, MCV is 62 fL and the smear shows target cells. Both parents have mild microcytosis without anemia.
oneliner: 7M + Mediterranean + well at birth, anemic by 6 months + hepatosplenomegaly + microcytic anemia with target cells + microcytic parents → which electrophoresis pattern?
ask: Which hemoglobin electrophoresis pattern is most likely?

options.E: No HbA; mainly HbF, raised HbA2

whyNot.A: **HbS** disease is normocytic; his MCV of 62 and microcytic parents point to a thalassemia
whyNot.B: **Mostly HbA** with mild HbA2 elevation is the carrier (minor) state, as in his parents
whyNot.C: **HbH** comes from loss of three alpha genes and is evident from the newborn period; he was well at birth and worsened as HbF fell
whyNot.D: **Hb Bart's** predominates in hydrops fetalis, which presents at birth

answer: No HbA; mostly HbF with raised HbA2 (beta-thalassemia major)
why: Beta chains are absent in both alleles, but the infant stays well until **fetal hemoglobin falls** at 6 to 9 months. Electrophoresis then shows **no HbA**, with **HbF and HbA2** carrying the oxygen, and the marrow expands with **hepatosplenomegaly** and facial bossing.

idea.rule: Beta-thalassemia major = no HbA, high HbF, high HbA2; presents after 6 months.

stem: A 55-year-old man has fatigue, frequent infections and a heavy feeling in the left upper abdomen. Examination shows a massive spleen and no enlarged lymph nodes. Counts show pancytopenia with very few monocytes. A marrow aspirate attempt yields no fluid. The blood film shows B cells with fine cytoplasmic projections.
oneliner: 55M + fatigue, infections + massive splenomegaly, no nodes + pancytopenia, low monocytes + dry tap + B cells with fine projections → which cytochemical stain is positive?
ask: Which cytochemical stain is most likely to be positive in the abnormal cells?

options.C: Periodic acid-Schiff in a block pattern

whyNot.A: **Myeloperoxidase** marks myeloid blasts of AML; these cells are mature B lymphocytes
whyNot.C: **PAS block positivity** is seen in lymphoblasts of ALL, not in mature B cells
whyNot.D: **LAP** is a neutrophil enzyme used to separate CML from a leukemoid reaction; these abnormal cells are B cells
whyNot.E: **Nonspecific esterase** marks monocytic cells (AML M4/M5); his monocytes are depleted

why: **Massive splenomegaly without nodes**, **pancytopenia with monocytopenia** and a **dry tap** from marrow fibrosis suggest **hairy cell leukemia**. These B cells have fine projections and stain for **TRAP**, together with CD11c, CD25 and CD103.

idea.rule: Hairy cell leukemia = B cell, TRAP positive, CD11c, CD25, CD103.

stem: A 22-year-old man has had bruising for two weeks, and his gums are swollen and bleed. Hemoglobin is 8 g/dL, platelets 35,000/mm3 and white cell count 14,000/mm3. The smear shows 42% blasts, some with needle-shaped red cytoplasmic rods. He has no lymph node enlargement.
oneliner: 22M + bruising + gum swelling and bleeding + pancytopenia + 42% blasts with Auer rods → which flow markers?
ask: Which flow cytometry markers are most likely on the blasts?

whyNot.A: **TdT, CD10 and CD19** mark B-lymphoblastic leukemia; Auer rods show a myeloid lineage
whyNot.B: **CD3 and CD7** mark T-lymphoblasts, which cause mediastinal masses in adolescents
whyNot.C: **CD11c, CD25 and CD103** are hairy cell leukemia, with mature cells and a big spleen
whyNot.E: **CD5 and CD23** mark CLL, a disease of older adults with mature small lymphocytes

answer: CD13 and CD33 (myeloid markers; acute myeloid leukemia)
why: **Blasts with Auer rods** and **gum infiltration** fit **AML**. Auer rods are fused **myeloperoxidase-containing** granules, and the blasts carry the myeloid markers **CD13 and CD33** (with CD117), not lymphoid markers like TdT or CD10.

idea.rule: AML = myeloperoxidase positive, CD13, CD33; ALL = TdT, CD10, CD19.
also: APL (M3): t(15;17), treat with all-trans retinoic acid

stem: A 28-year-old man develops a swollen, painful right calf after a 14-hour flight, and a duplex scan shows a popliteal vein clot. His mother had a leg clot during pregnancy. Before any anticoagulant is given, PT, PTT and platelet count are normal, and antithrombin activity is normal.
oneliner: 28M + DVT after long flight + mother had pregnancy clot + normal PT, PTT, platelets, antithrombin → which lab result?
ask: Which laboratory result most likely points to the underlying defect?

options.A: Clotting time not lengthened by added activated protein C
options.B: Prolonged PTT that does not correct with mixing
options.C: PTT that fails to rise despite high-dose heparin
options.D: Platelet fall of more than 50% after a week
options.E: Prolonged PT that corrects with vitamin K

whyNot.B: **Non-correcting prolonged PTT** is lupus anticoagulant; his PTT is normal
whyNot.C: **Heparin resistance** is antithrombin deficiency; his antithrombin activity is normal
whyNot.D: **Platelet fall after heparin** is HIT; he has had no heparin and his platelets are normal
whyNot.E: **PT corrected by vitamin K** reflects vitamin K lack, a bleeding problem; his PT is normal

answer: Resistance to activated protein C: clotting time not lengthened when APC is added (factor V Leiden)
why: A **provoked DVT in a young man** with a **family history of clots** and normal screening tests suggests an inherited thrombophilia. In **factor V Leiden** the mutant factor V (Arg506Gln) **resists cleavage by activated protein C**, so adding APC fails to prolong clotting, the **APC resistance** result.

idea.rule: Factor V Leiden = APC resistance; the commonest inherited thrombophilia.
also: Protein C deficiency predisposes to warfarin skin necrosis
Antiphospholipid syndrome prolongs PTT that does not correct on mixing

stem: A 15-year-old girl had an allogeneic marrow transplant from her brother one year ago for relapsed acute myeloid leukemia. She now feels well, and her blood counts are normal. A routine marrow aspirate is sent for chromosome analysis, and the karyotype reads 46,XY in all cells examined.
oneliner: 15F + allogeneic marrow transplant from brother for AML 1 year ago + well, normal counts + marrow karyotype 46,XY → which explanation?
ask: Which explanation best fits the karyotype result?

whyNot.A: **Relapse** would show her own 46,XX leukemic cells, and her counts are normal
whyNot.C: **Male pseudohermaphroditism** would give 46,XY in every tissue from birth, not only in marrow after a male donor transplant
whyNot.D: **Radiation** causes breaks and translocations, not a whole change of sex chromosomes
whyNot.E: **Myelodysplasia** is an abnormal clone from the recipient, which would be 46,XX

answer: Successful engraftment of the male donor's marrow
why: After an **allogeneic transplant** the marrow is replaced by the **donor's cells**. A female recipient with a **46,XY marrow** and normal counts means the brother's stem cells have **engrafted**; recurrence would show her own **46,XX** cells.

idea.rule: Donor-sex karyotype in the marrow = engraftment; recipient-sex karyotype = relapse or graft failure.
also: Allogeneic: donor differs; autologous: own cells
HLA matching of donor and recipient
